implementation_notes: std::shared_mutex is the default: lock_shared/try_lock_shared/unlock_shared for readers and lock/try_lock for writers, wrapped in std::shared_lock and std::unique_lock so release happens on every exit path; C++14 codebases use std::shared_timed_mutex, which the same guards accept. Choose it where reads dominate and sections are long enough that serialising readers shows up; for short sections a plain std::mutex with std::lock_guard is usually faster, because shared_mutex is larger and its shared path is not free.
pitfalls: std::shared_mutex allows only one lock (shared or exclusive) per thread at a time; taking a shared_lock and then a unique_lock on the same mutex in one thread deadlocks.
Do not use the raw lock()/unlock() pairs without a guard: an exception between them leaves the mutex locked for good.
Fairness is not guaranteed; writer starvation is implementation-defined, so a reader-dominated loop can postpone a refresh indefinitely.
shared_mutex/shared_timed_mutex are larger and can be slower than std::mutex for short sections - measure before replacing a plain mutex.

variants.name: Boost.Thread shared_mutex (pre-C++17, portable)
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Thread mirrors the std API on C++11 toolchains and adds upgrade_mutex with upgrade_lock, which allows a held read lock to be upgraded to a write lock without releasing it - the feature the standard never adopted. Choose it for portability or when a genuine upgrade path is required; with C++17 available the std type is the better default.
pitfalls: boost::shared_mutex has no upgrade support; upgrade is a property of the separate boost::upgrade_mutex type.
Only one upgrade lock may exist per boost::upgrade_mutex, and upgrading while other readers hold the lock blocks until they leave.
Boost.Thread must be linked (the locking types are not header-only in modern Boost).

variants.name: POSIX pthread_rwlock_t behind a C++ RAII guard
variants.implementation_notes: Wrap the C primitive in two small guards when the toolchain has neither C++17 nor Boost, or when the lock must be shared with a C core: pthread_rwlock_rdlock/wrlock/unlock behind constructors and destructors restores the RAII discipline the C API lacks. This is also the only realisation that can be placed in shared memory (PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED).
pitfalls: No upgrade support: release the read lock before taking the write lock.
The default glibc policy is read-preferring; set PTHREAD_RWLOCK_PREFER_WRITER_NONRECURSIVE_NP when writers must not starve (and accept that recursive read locking then deadlocks).
The rwlock must be destroyed before its memory is reused, and guards must not outlive it.
